record.paper_title: Open problems in Euclidean Ramsey Theory
record.original_question: Let N be the set of natural numbers. If A is a subset of N and the reciprocal sum Σ_{a in A} 1/a diverges, must A contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length? The source also notes that it was not even known whether this hypothesis forces a 3-term arithmetic progression.

evidence.quote: then A must contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions
not even known if this hypothesis implies that A has a 3-term arithmetic progression

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ denote the set of positive integers. A finite arithmetic progression of length $k$ is a set of the form $\{a, a+d, a+2d, \dots, a+(k-1)d\}$ with $a\in\mathbb{N}$ and $d\in\mathbb{N}$.

Prove or disprove: For every subset $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ satisfying
$$\sum_{a\in A}\frac{1}{a}=\infty,$$
and for every integer $k\geq 3$, the set $A$ contains an arithmetic progression of length $k$.

(The special case $k=3$ asks whether divergence of the reciprocal sum already forces the existence of three distinct elements $a,b,c\in A$ with $b-a=c-b>0$.)
artifact.status_search_result: The full conjecture (arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions) remains open. The case k=3 was resolved in 2020 by Bloom and Sisask, who proved that any set A ⊂ {1,…,N} with no nontrivial 3-term arithmetic progression has size ≪ N/(log N)^{1+c}, which is enough to imply that any A ⊆ ℕ with divergent reciprocal sum contains a 3-term arithmetic progression. The cases k ≥ 4 are still open.

status_evidence.title: Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The conjecture states that if the sum of reciprocals of a set of positive integers diverges, then it contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions; it remains open in general.

status_evidence.title: Landmark Math Proof Clears Hurdle in Top Erdős Conjecture (Quanta)
status_evidence.snippet: Bloom and Sisask proved that any set whose reciprocal sum diverges must contain infinitely many 3-term arithmetic progressions.

status_evidence.title: Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions
status_evidence.snippet: If A ⊂ {1,...,N} contains no non-trivial three-term arithmetic progressions then |A| ≪ N/(log N)^{1+c}, proving the first non-trivial case of Erdős's conjecture on arithmetic progressions.
